Dinner comes prepared by an Italian chef who mingles his home country's techniques with Caribbean flavors. You can start with octopus salad with potatoes and chickpeas, then make your way down the menu to pappardelle with a nutmeg cream sauce. It won't be the last time you see nutmeg on a menu here. Founded in the late 17th century, the capital city of St. George’s lies on the island’s southwest coast. Sailboats sway at anchor in Clarkes Court Bay, while lights flicker against the dark green hills. The island’s hidden treasure is its views—and they are not limited to quaint seaside cafés.

Consider the nearby resort of Laluna on Portici Bay. With 16 hillside cottages nestled around a private cove beach, the property abounds with scenic panoramas. Founded by a former Italian fashion consultant, Laluna is chic without being pretentious—a stylish retreat on one of the Caribbean’s quietest islands.

Eco-inspired rooms feature fabric-draped four-poster beds from Bali, private plunge pools, and bamboo-topped verandas. Even the most distant cottage is only 150 feet from the beach, making Laluna the kind of place designed for barefoot lounging.

Ultracasual dress code aside, Laluna takes dining seriously. Dinner is prepared by an Italian chef who blends the techniques of his homeland with Caribbean flavors. Begin with an octopus salad served with potatoes and chickpeas, then work your way through the menu to pappardelle with nutmeg cream sauce.

It will not be the last time you encounter nutmeg on a menu here. Grenada supplies one-third of the world’s nutmeg, which can be sampled as a powder, syrup, or jam. Almost every visitor brings some home, usually in a small basket also filled with cloves, cinnamon, mace, bay leaves, and ginger. The country may not boast flashy casinos or high-rise resorts, but Grenada grows more spices per square mile than anywhere else in the world.

### Coastal Living: The Other Caribbean

Producing these flavors requires a lush climate, such as that found in the rainforest at Grenada’s center. Grand Etang National Park preserves the island’s tropical flora and fauna. Visitors can book guides to lead them through terraced banana farms and forests of giant gommier trees, teak, and wild orchids. From a mountain peak, 90 percent of the island is visible, glowing vivid green after a midday rain.

As one might expect, the cities here move at a sleepy island pace. But the township of Gouyave, on Grenada’s western coast, springs to life on Fish Fridays—part street-food festival, part outdoor concert, and part extended-family gathering.

Beginning in the late afternoon, the fishing village’s streets and side passages fill with tables laden with seafood. Vendors sell sample-size servings of everything from lobster and jerked marlin to deep-fried fish cakes. Music lifts the spirit, as do the enthusiastic greetings exchanged among friends and relatives.

Visitors to Gouyave are often reluctant to leave. Eventually, however, they return to Laluna along a cliffside road illuminated by stars on a cloudless night—yet another unforgettable view.

Laluna’s cliffside cottages start at $390. Rates do not include meals, but all snorkeling and kayaking are included. Call 866/452-5862 or visit **laluna.com**.

Guided hikes from Henry’s Safari Tours cost $40 to $55 per person. Denis Henry offers excursions tailored to your experience level, and his taxi tours are also the best on the island. Call 347/721-9271 or visit **henrysafari.com**.

Reservations at Little Dipper on Clarkes Court Bay in Woburn can be made through Laluna or by calling 473/444-5136.

From Laluna, a round-trip taxi to Fish Fridays in Gouyave costs roughly $100. Food at the festival costs between $15 and $20 per person.

## Grenada: The Caribbean’s Quietly Luxurious Spice Island

Grenada reveals itself gradually. Unlike Caribbean destinations defined by high-rise resorts, glittering casinos, and crowded nightlife, this small island offers a quieter kind of pleasure. Its appeal lies in green hills descending toward secluded bays, restaurants positioned above the sea, intimate resorts tucked into tropical gardens, and a cuisine shaped by both Caribbean abundance and international influence.

The best way to experience Grenada is often from a table with a view. Across the island, scenic restaurants make the landscape part of the meal. Terraces overlook fishing boats and blue-green water, while hillside dining rooms capture the evening breeze and the fading light. The atmosphere is generally relaxed rather than theatrical. Even in the island’s more refined establishments, luxury tends to feel personal and unforced.

Grenadian cooking begins with the island’s remarkable natural abundance. Warm waters provide fresh fish and shellfish, while the fertile interior produces citrus, mangoes, coconuts, plantains, cocoa, and a wide range of herbs and spices. Nutmeg is the island’s most famous crop, so important to Grenada’s identity that it appears on the national flag. Mace, cinnamon, cloves, ginger, turmeric, and bay leaves also flourish in the tropical climate, scenting markets, kitchens, and roadside stalls.

These ingredients give local dishes a distinctive depth. Fish may be grilled simply and served with lime, vegetables, or spicy sauces, while stews and curries carry the warmth of locally grown seasonings. Grenada’s national dish, oil down, brings together breadfruit, coconut milk, vegetables, spices, and salted meat or fish in a rich one-pot meal. Its name refers to the coconut milk cooking down and leaving behind its flavorful oils.

The island’s culinary character is not limited to traditional Caribbean food. One of its most appealing expressions is the meeting of Caribbean ingredients and Italian technique. Pasta, risotto, and seafood preparations take on new life when made with local produce, herbs, and freshly caught fish. The combination feels natural: both traditions value direct flavors, seasonal ingredients, and meals meant to be enjoyed slowly. A plate might pair handmade pasta with lobster or prawns, or bring tropical fruit and Grenadian chocolate into a familiar European dessert.

Grenada’s small resorts reflect the same preference for intimacy and restraint. Rather than separating guests from the island behind vast walls and sprawling developments, many properties are designed on a human scale. Villas and cottages sit among palms and flowering plants, and rooms open toward gardens, beaches, or broad ocean views. Service is attentive without being formal, creating the feeling of a private retreat rather than a conventional resort complex.

This unpretentious approach to luxury is central to Grenada’s charm. Comfort is present, but it rarely demands attention. The real extravagances are space, silence, warm water, fresh food, and the ability to watch the horizon without interruption. Days can be organized around swimming, sailing, snorkeling, or spa treatments, but they can just as easily pass over a long lunch or a walk along an uncrowded beach.

Beyond the coast, the landscape becomes even more vivid. Mountain roads wind through dense vegetation, past waterfalls, farms, and villages where spices are grown, dried, and sold. The air itself can seem fragrant. Nutmeg shells, cocoa beans, cinnamon bark, and bundles of herbs offer a sensory introduction to the agricultural traditions that earned Grenada the nickname “the Spice Isle.”

Spice production is more than a picturesque detail. It has long shaped the island’s economy, cuisine, and international identity. Grenada is among the world’s most prominent producers of nutmeg and mace, an extraordinary distinction for a country of its size. Visiting a plantation, processing station, or local market shows how closely the island’s celebrated flavors are connected to the work of farmers and producers.

Chocolate has also become an important part of Grenada’s food culture. Cocoa grown in the island’s rich soil is transformed into bars and confections with complex flavors, often complemented by nutmeg, sea salt, or other local ingredients. Together, cocoa and spices demonstrate how Grenada can turn agricultural heritage into experiences that appeal to modern travelers without losing their local character.

Ultimately, Grenada’s greatest strength is its refusal to compete with the Caribbean’s flashiest destinations. It does not need monumental hotels or nonstop entertainment to hold a visitor’s attention. Its pleasures are subtler: a hidden table above the sea, a carefully prepared plate of pasta and local seafood, the scent of nutmeg in a market, or the sight of forested hills glowing in late-afternoon light.

For travelers seeking spectacle, other islands may offer louder attractions. Grenada offers something more intimate—a landscape to be absorbed slowly, food rooted in place, and luxury measured not by grandeur but by calm.

# The Art of Coastal Living

Coastal living is more than residing near the sea—it is a lifestyle shaped by fresh air, open spaces, and the calming rhythm of the waves. Mornings often begin with soft sunlight over the water, while evenings invite quiet walks along the shore.

The coastal aesthetic reflects this relaxed atmosphere through natural materials, light colors, and airy interiors. Linen fabrics, weathered wood, woven textures, and shades of blue create spaces that feel comfortable and connected to nature. Large windows and outdoor areas allow sea breezes and natural light to become part of everyday life.

Yet the true appeal of coastal living lies in its slower, more mindful pace. It encourages people to appreciate simple pleasures: fresh seafood, sandy paths, changing tides, and time spent with family and friends. Whether enjoyed year-round or during a seaside escape, the coastal lifestyle offers a refreshing balance of beauty, comfort, and tranquility.

counterfactuals.output:
# Grenada, Seasoned by the Sea

*On the Spice Isle, a barefoot stay at Laluna leads to rainforest trails, nutmeg-scented roads, and a Friday-night fish feast.*

Grenada announces itself before the wheels touch down. Green hills fold toward cobalt bays, fishing boats idle close to shore, and the air—warm, humid, faintly floral—seems to carry a pinch of spice.

The southern Caribbean island is famous for nutmeg, but its appeal is layered: quiet beaches, an emerald interior, villages where roadside stands sell cocoa balls and cinnamon bark, and a food culture that shifts easily from handmade pasta to paper plates piled with grilled lobster. Grenada feels polished in places, wonderfully unvarnished in others—and best when a trip includes both.

## Barefoot Ease at Laluna

Tucked into a hillside above a secluded cove near Morne Rouge, **Laluna** is the sort of retreat that makes shoes seem unnecessary. The intimate resort’s cottages and villas are set among tropical foliage, with private plunge pools, canopied beds, and decks angled toward the Caribbean. The mood is more private hideaway than grand hotel: morning yoga, a swim before breakfast, perhaps an afternoon treatment at the Asian-inspired spa.

At the water’s edge, Laluna’s **Little Dipper** restaurant brings an Italian sensibility to Grenadian ingredients. Expect dishes such as fresh fish with herbs and citrus, house-made pasta, salads brightened with local fruit, and desserts that make good use of the island’s chocolate and spices. Order a rum punch at sunset, when the bay turns copper and the palms become silhouettes.

Laluna is romantic without feeling overly formal, though its steep paths and steps may be challenging for travelers with limited mobility.

**Typical cost:** Cottage rates commonly begin around **US$500–$700 per night** in lower-demand periods and can rise above **US$900** in winter; larger villas cost considerably more. Taxes and service charges may add roughly **20%–25%**. At Little Dipper, budget about **US$20–$30 for lunch entrées** and **US$30–$50 for dinner mains**, before drinks, tax, and service. Resort packages may include breakfast or other meals.

## Into the Green

Grenada’s beaches are seductive, but the island’s interior provides its deeper pulse. About an hour from the southwest coast, **Grand Etang National Park and Forest Reserve** surrounds a crater lake high in the central mountains. Ferns crowd the road, bamboo arches overhead, and clouds can arrive without warning.

The lake itself is an easy stop, but walkers should continue onto one of the reserve’s trails. Short routes pass through rainforest alive with tree frogs, hummingbirds, and Mona monkeys, while more strenuous excursions lead toward waterfalls and ridgelines. Nearby Seven Sisters Falls is a popular guided hike, particularly after rain, when the forest becomes slick and brilliantly green.

Bring real walking shoes rather than beach sandals, plus water, insect repellent, and a light rain jacket. Trails can be muddy, and signage is not always comprehensive.

**Typical cost:** Entry or visitor fees are generally only a few dollars—allow about **EC$5–$10 (US$2–$4)**, depending on the site. A local guide for a short hike may cost roughly **US$40–$80 per person**, with private transfers or longer excursions priced higher.

## Friday Night in Gouyave

On Friday evening, the west-coast fishing town of **Gouyave** turns dinner into a street party. At **Fish Friday**, vendors set up beneath simple awnings and serve whatever came from the sea: grilled snapper, fried flying fish, fish cakes, conch, shrimp skewers, lobster when available, and bowls of rich seafood broth. Tables fill quickly, music drifts between the stalls, and smoke from the grills perfumes the narrow streets.

Come hungry and graze rather than committing to a single plate. A cold Carib beer pairs well with almost everything; so does fresh lime juice. The atmosphere usually gathers after 6 p.m. and becomes liveliest around 7:30 or 8.

**Typical cost:** Snacks such as fish cakes may run **EC$5–$10 (US$2–$4)**; seafood plates generally cost **EC$25–$60 (US$9–$22)**. Lobster and larger portions can be more. Carry Eastern Caribbean dollars and small bills, as not every vendor accepts cards.

## Following the Spice Route

Grenada’s nickname—**the Spice Isle**—is not a marketing flourish. Nutmeg trees grow across the island, producing both nutmeg and its lacy red outer covering, mace. Cinnamon, cloves, bay leaves, turmeric, ginger, and allspice thrive here too, while cocoa has become an increasingly important part of Grenada’s agricultural identity.

In Gouyave, the **Gouyave Nutmeg Processing Station** offers a glimpse of the sorting, grading, and packing process that has supported local families for generations. Elsewhere, estates and small producers demonstrate how cacao pods become chocolate bars and how spices move from tree to kitchen.

Look for whole nutmeg, mace, cinnamon bark, cocoa tea balls, and locally made chocolate. Whole spices travel better and retain their fragrance longer than preground versions. Check your home country’s customs rules before packing fresh plant products.

**Typical cost:** Short spice or processing-station visits often cost **US$2–$10**. Estate tours generally range from **US$10–$30 per adult**. Small bags of spices cost about **US$3–$8**, while Grenadian chocolate bars typically run **US$4–$10**.

---

## Plan Your Grenada Trip

### When to go
The driest, busiest period is generally **December through April**, with correspondingly higher hotel rates. **May and June** can offer a good balance of lower prices and manageable rainfall. The wettest months usually fall between **June and November**. Grenada lies near the southern edge of the Atlantic hurricane belt, but travelers should still consider insurance during hurricane season.

### Getting there
Maurice Bishop International Airport is near the main hotel area in southwest Grenada. Direct or connecting flights operate from several Caribbean, U.S., Canadian, and U.K. gateways, with schedules varying by season.

A taxi from the airport to Laluna generally takes **15–25 minutes** and may cost about **US$25–$40**, depending on luggage and time of day. Confirm the fare before departure or arrange a resort transfer.

### Getting around
Driving is on the **left**, roads are narrow and winding, and travel times are longer than distances suggest. Rental cars typically start around **US$60–$90 per day**, plus fuel and the local driving permit. Visitors uncomfortable with steep roads may prefer taxis or a private driver.

A full-day private island tour commonly costs **US$200–$350 per vehicle**, depending on the route and number of passengers. Public minibuses are inexpensive—often just a few Eastern Caribbean dollars—but are best suited to flexible travelers without tight schedules.

### Money
Grenada uses the **Eastern Caribbean dollar**, fixed at approximately **EC$2.70 to US$1**. U.S. dollars are widely accepted, though change may be returned in local currency. Carry cash for markets, buses, trail guides, and Fish Friday.

### What to pack
Bring reef-safe sunscreen, mosquito repellent, sturdy walking shoes, a rain shell, swimwear, and a light sweater for air-conditioned interiors. A small dry bag is useful for boat trips and sudden tropical showers.

*All prices are approximate and can change with season, availability, taxes, and service charges; confirm directly before booking.*

# Grenada at an Easy Pace  
### Nutmeg-scented hills, rainforest trails and Caribbean-Italian dinners make the Spice Isle an ideal escape for travelers seeking beauty without bustle.

Morning arrives softly in Grenada. Sunlight spreads across the calm water at Morne Rouge Bay, fishing boats rock beyond the sand, and the green hills behind St. George’s glow beneath a passing veil of cloud. There is no urgent itinerary here—only the promise of a swim, a good meal and perhaps a road winding into the rainforest.

Known as the Spice Isle, Grenada feels both lush and intimate. Nutmeg, cinnamon, cloves and cocoa thrive in its volcanic soil, perfuming markets and roadside stands. In St. George’s, the capital’s pastel buildings rise around a horseshoe-shaped harbor, while vendors display strings of nutmeg, jars of preserves and fragrant spice blends. Crack open a nutmeg fruit and you may see the crimson lace of mace wrapped around the dark seed—a vivid reminder that Grenada’s signature crop is more than a souvenir.

Beyond the coast, the island becomes cooler and wilder. Trails around Grand Etang National Park lead through ferns, bamboo and dense tropical forest, where mona monkeys rustle in the canopy and mist drifts over the crater lake. The walk to Seven Sisters Falls rewards hikers with freshwater pools and cascades framed by glossy foliage. For a quieter outing, the paths near Concord Falls offer mountain views, spice trees and inviting places to pause beside the water.

Back at sea level, Grenada’s beaches encourage long, unstructured afternoons. Grand Anse is the island’s celebrated sweep of pale sand, but travelers seeking greater solitude can settle into sheltered Morne Rouge or explore the coves around Lance aux Épines. On the north coast, waves meet darker volcanic shores, and near Sauteurs the sea appears especially dramatic, stretching toward the Grenadine islands.

Grenada’s cuisine is equally shaped by its landscape. Local kitchens serve oil down—the national dish, traditionally combining breadfruit, coconut milk, callaloo, dumplings and salted meat—as well as grilled snapper, conch, lobster and spiced fish straight from nearby boats. Nutmeg finds its way into rum punches, cakes, sauces and ice cream, lending even familiar flavors a distinctly Grenadian warmth.

The island also has a surprising Caribbean-Italian streak. At intimate restaurants and boutique hotels, Italian technique meets tropical produce in dishes such as lobster linguine with Scotch bonnet, callaloo ravioli, wood-fired pizza topped with local herbs, and panna cotta scented with nutmeg or cocoa. A chilled glass of wine, handmade pasta and a table overlooking the Caribbean make an elegant counterpoint to barefoot lunches of grilled fish.

For a livelier taste of local life, head to Gouyave Fish Friday, when the west-coast fishing town fills with open-air stalls and the aroma of frying seafood. Snapper, tuna, shrimp, lobster and fish cakes are served alongside plantains, breadfruit and cold drinks, with music carrying through the streets. It has the atmosphere of a neighborhood seafood festival: convivial, flavorful and rooted in the island’s fishing traditions.

Yet Grenada’s greatest pleasure may be the space it leaves between experiences. A rainforest hike can end with a nap by the sea. A market visit can become a slow lunch. Sunset might be watched from the hills above St. George’s, where the harbor turns gold and the boats become silhouettes.

On the Spice Isle, quiet is not the absence of activity. It is the luxury of noticing—the scent of grated nutmeg, the flash of a waterfall through the trees, the taste of lobster tangled with fresh pasta, and the Caribbean folding gently onto the shore.

# Grenada: Cottages, Coves and Friday-Night Fish

Grenada rewards travelers who slow down. Beyond the beaches and spice markets, the island’s pleasures lie in hillside hideaways, quiet bays, back-road adventures and seafood served straight from the grill.

## Stay: Laluna’s Cliffside Cottages

Tucked into a wooded hillside near Morne Rouge, **Laluna** feels deliberately removed from Grenada’s larger resorts. Its Italian-Caribbean aesthetic—dark wood, gauzy linens and open-air living spaces—sets a romantic tone, while individual cottages descend toward a small, secluded beach.

Private verandas and plunge pools make it easy to stay in, but the sea below provides a compelling reason to venture out. Days here revolve around swimming, paddleboarding, spa treatments and sunset drinks. Laluna is especially well suited to couples seeking privacy, though its steep paths and hillside layout may be challenging for travelers with limited mobility.

## A Bay Retreat: Little Dipper on Clarkes Court Bay

On Grenada’s quieter southern coast, **Little Dipper** overlooks **Clarkes Court Bay**, a broad, protected harbor known for sailboats, mangroves and a slower pace than nearby Grand Anse. The setting offers a more residential experience: mornings over the water, unhurried meals and easy access to the island’s marinas and southern beaches.

A car is useful here. Clarkes Court Bay is peaceful rather than central, making it a good base for travelers who want independence and don’t mind driving to restaurants, shops and swimming beaches.

## Explore: Henry’s Safari Tours

To understand why Grenada is called the Spice Isle, head inland with **Henry’s Safari Tours**. Excursions typically leave the coast behind for narrow mountain roads, rainforest scenery, waterfalls, villages and agricultural stops where nutmeg, cocoa, cinnamon and other tropical crops are grown.

The appeal is as much the journey as the destination. A knowledgeable local guide can connect the landscape with Grenada’s history and explain how farming, fishing and village life shape the island. Wear comfortable shoes, carry rain protection and expect winding roads. Tour routes and inclusions can vary, so confirm the itinerary directly when booking.

## Friday Night in Gouyave

On Friday evening, the west-coast fishing town of **Gouyave** becomes one of Grenada’s liveliest dining destinations. During **Fish Friday**, vendors set up stalls along the streets and serve seafood in almost every form: grilled fish, fried snapper, fish cakes, shrimp, lobster when available, and local specialties accompanied by provisions, sauces and cold drinks.

Arrive hungry and sample several smaller dishes rather than committing to one plate. The atmosphere is casual and communal, with music, smoke from the grills and a mix of residents and visitors circulating between stalls. Bring cash, and consider arranging transportation in advance if you plan to drink or are staying on the opposite side of the island. Schedules can change around holidays or special events, so verify locally before setting out.

## A Suggested Grenada Day

Begin with a late breakfast overlooking the water at Laluna or Little Dipper. Spend the afternoon touring the rainforest and spice-growing interior with Henry’s Safari Tours, then follow the west coast north to Gouyave for Fish Friday. The return drive is easiest with a driver, particularly after dark.

# Island Info

- **Country:** Grenada, including the sister islands of Carriacou and Petite Martinique  
- **Capital:** St. George’s  
- **Currency:** Eastern Caribbean dollar; U.S. dollars are widely accepted, though change may be given in local currency  
- **Language:** English; Grenadian Creole is also spoken  
- **Getting there:** Maurice Bishop International Airport serves the main island  
- **Getting around:** Rental cars, taxis and local minibuses are available. Driving is on the left, and many roads are narrow, steep and winding  
- **Best time to visit:** The drier months generally run from January through May; rain is more frequent from June through December  
- **What to pack:** Light clothing, reef-conscious sun protection, insect repellent, rain gear and sturdy footwear for waterfalls or rainforest walks  
- **Reservations:** Book Laluna, Little Dipper, tours and Friday-night transportation in advance during busy periods  
- **Good to know:** Confirm current opening times, tour schedules and Fish Friday arrangements directly before traveling, as details may change seasonally.
